Circle of fifths. A geometric diagram organizing all twelve pitches in their major and minor keys in a circle, ordered by their distance in perfect fifths. It is an indispensable tool for understanding key relationships, chord progressions, and modulation, and it appears on nearly every musician's wall.

Clockwise from C, each step moves up a perfect fifth: C to G to D to A to E to B to F sharp. This progression adds one sharp to the key signature with each step. Moving counterclockwise goes down a fifth, adding flats instead. Adjacent keys on the circle share the most pitches and are the closest in harmonic color. Moving around the circle increases harmonic distance.

The outer ring shows major keys while the inner ring shows relative minor keys, each sharing the same key signature. Key signatures follow the circle predictably: zero sharps or flats at C and A minor, one sharp (F sharp) at G and E minor, one flat (B flat) at F and D minor. Musicians use the circle to quickly find closely related keys for modulation, predict the next chord in a progression—many pop and jazz songs follow a clockwise path like four, one, five or D minor, G, C—and memorize key signatures. The circle represents the harmonic space of the major and minor tonal system, and adjacent keys on the circle are the easiest to modulate into for smooth harmonic transitions.
